title: Non-Trading Organisation
tagline: Receipts and payments, income and expenditure, and the closing balance sheet of clubs, societies and institutions.

overview.intro: A school, a hospital, a library or a sports club does not buy goods to sell them, so gross profit has no meaning for it. Its purpose is service rather than profit, and its accounts are built around three statements instead. The receipts and payments account is a summary of the cash book, showing every inflow and outflow on both sides regardless of which year it belongs to. The income and expenditure account is the accrual equivalent of a profit and loss account, and only the surplus or deficit of the period belongs in it. The closing balance sheet then shows the funds the organisation holds on the last day, including accumulated capital funds.

facts.label: Receipts and payments
facts.value: A cash summary: receipts on the debit side, payments on the credit side, opening balance brought down and closing balance carried down.

facts.label: Income and expenditure
facts.value: Accrual statement: revenue income of the period less revenue expenditure of the period; the balance is surplus or deficit.

facts.label: Capital items
facts.value: Life membership fees, legacies, donations for buildings and tournament receipts go to the balance sheet, never to income and expenditure.

facts.label: Exam weight
facts.value: A receipts and payments problem with a subscription schedule is the standard ten-mark question in this unit.

learningOutcomes: Explain the purpose and nature of a non-trading organisation.
Prepare a receipts and payments account from a cash book.
Prepare an income and expenditure account on the accrual basis.
Prepare a closing balance sheet showing the capital fund.
Distinguish capital and revenue items in the receipts of such an organisation.

blocks.text: A non-trading organisation is one formed not to earn profit for its members but to provide a service, such as education, healthcare, culture, religion or sport. Its members pay subscriptions, it receives grants and donations, and it spends on the service it exists to provide. Because there are no owners seeking a return, the accounting objective changes from profit measurement to stewardship: showing honestly what was received, what was spent, and what funds remain for the next period. The equivalent of capital is the capital fund, built up from accumulated surpluses over the years.

items.meaning: Periodic amount paid by members to keep their membership, the main recurring income.
One-time payment for permanent membership; a capital receipt.
Amount received under a will; a capital receipt.
Accumulated surplus of past years, the non-trading equivalent of capital.
Excess of income over expenditure for the period, added to the capital fund.
Excess of expenditure over income for the period, deducted from the capital fund.

blocks.text: The receipts and payments account is the summarised cash book of the organisation. Every sum received during the period, whether capital or revenue and whether it belongs to this year or an earlier one, appears on the debit side. Every sum paid appears on the credit side. The opening cash and bank balance is brought down at the top of the debit side and the closing balance is carried down at the foot of the credit side, so the account begins and ends with a cash position. Because it is a cash record, it makes no adjustment for outstanding or prepaid amounts, and it does not distinguish between money spent on a durable asset and money spent on running the year.

blocks.caption: Receipts and payments account for the year ended 31 December

items: All receipts appear on the debit side and all payments on the credit side.
Capital and revenue items are mixed, because cash does not distinguish them.
Opening and closing cash and bank balances frame the account.
No accrual, outstanding or prepaid adjustment is made.
Cheques issued but not presented are treated as payments still outstanding in the bank.

blocks.text: The income and expenditure account is the accrual counterpart of the profit and loss account and reports only the revenue of this period. On the credit side goes every income earned in the period, including subscriptions due for this year whether received or not, and excluding any capital receipt or advance. On the debit side goes every expense incurred in the period, including amounts outstanding at the year end and excluding any payment that relates to another period. Depreciation on assets owned is charged here as well. The balance is a surplus, which is added to the capital fund, or a deficit, which is deducted from it.

The conversion from the receipts and payments account is made by adjusting three things: cash items that belong to another period are removed, amounts earned or incurred but not received or paid are added, and non-revenue items such as legacies and life membership fees are taken out to the balance sheet. Subscription questions usually give amounts due in three different years, and the rule is to include only the amount relating to the current accounting period.

blocks.caption: Conversion rules from cash to accrual
rows: Subscription received in advance for next year
Subscription due but not received for this year
Subscription received for a prior year
Add to the expense and show as a liability
Deduct from the expense and show as an asset
Life membership fee, legacy, donation for a building
Exclude entirely; take to the balance sheet

items.text: Subscriptions of ₹2,00,000 received, ₹5,000 for last year, ₹8,000 for next year, ₹6,000 still due.
Salaries paid ₹90,000 with ₹7,000 outstanding and ₹4,000 prepaid.
items.note: Charge 90,000 + 7,000 − 4,000 = ₹93,000 to the income and expenditure account.

blocks.text: The closing balance sheet of a non-trading organisation starts with the capital fund as it stood at the beginning of the period, adds the surplus or deducts the deficit, adds the proceeds of life membership fees, legacies and specific donations that are capital in nature, and then lists the assets and liabilities held on the closing day. It has no share capital and no drawings, and the capital fund grows only through accumulated surpluses and capital receipts. Current assets such as subscriptions due and prepaid expenses appear alongside fixed assets such as the building, equipment and investments.

blocks.caption: Closing balance sheet as at 31 December

items: Open with the capital fund brought forward from the last balance sheet.
Add the surplus or deduct the deficit of the income and expenditure account.
Add life membership fees, legacies and donations for specific durable purposes.
Show subscriptions due as an asset and subscriptions in advance as a liability.
The account is drawn up on the liabilities and assets format, not in T form.

blocks.text: A complete problem supplies a receipts and payments account plus a few adjustment facts and asks for the income and expenditure account and the closing balance sheet. The efficient route is to work from the cash summary to the accrual statement line by line, and then to build the balance sheet from the opening capital fund. Start by listing each receipt and decide: does it belong to this period, is it capital or revenue, and is it fully earned? The same test applies to each payment. Once the surplus or deficit is known, every figure taken out of the income and expenditure account must reappear somewhere in the balance sheet, because no amount is simply discarded.

items: Classify each receipt as revenue of this year, capital, advance for a later year, or relating to an earlier year.
Adjust each expense for amounts outstanding or prepaid at the year end.
Charge depreciation on owned assets as an expenditure of the period.
Transfer the surplus to the capital fund and list all assets and liabilities at the closing date.
Check that subscriptions outstanding appear as an asset and subscriptions in advance as a liability.

items.text: Equipment purchased during the year ₹75,000 is a payment in the cash account but an asset in the balance sheet.
items.note: It is never charged to income and expenditure; only its yearly depreciation is.

items.text: A donation of ₹1,00,000 received for a new pavilion.
items.note: It is a capital receipt and stays out of income and expenditure until the pavilion is built and depreciated.

keyPoints: A non-trading organisation exists to provide service, not to earn profit for members.
Its capital equivalent is the capital fund, built from accumulated surpluses and capital receipts.
The receipts and payments account summarises the cash book without any accrual adjustment.
Capital receipts such as life membership fees, legacies and specific donations go to the balance sheet.
The income and expenditure account is prepared on the accrual basis for the current period only.
Subscriptions in advance are a liability; subscriptions due but not received are an asset.
The balance of the income and expenditure account is a surplus or a deficit.
Depreciation on owned assets is charged to the income and expenditure account.
The closing balance sheet begins with the opening capital fund adjusted by the surplus or deficit.
No amount leaving the income and expenditure account disappears: each appears in the balance sheet.
examFocus: Subscription questions carry the most marks: split the cash received into prior year, current year and next year before anything else.
Never charge the purchase of an asset to income and expenditure; only its depreciation belongs there.
Build the balance sheet from the capital fund and reconcile every excluded item, because a missing figure is the commonest lost mark.

vocabulary.meaning: Body formed to provide a service rather than profit to its members.
Recurring payment by a member to retain membership rights.
Summarised cash account listing all inflows and outflows of the period.
Accrual statement of revenue income less revenue expenditure for the period.
Accumulated surplus of prior years, the equivalent of capital in a non-trading body.
Excess of income over expenditure in the period, added to the capital fund.
Amount received under a will, treated as a capital receipt.

questions.prompt: The receipts and payments account is:
options: An accrual statement of the period’s earnings
A summary of the cash book showing all cash inflows and outflows
A statement of assets and liabilities only
A record of capital transactions only
questions.answer: A summary of the cash book showing all cash inflows and outflows
questions.explanation: It is a cash summary covering every receipt and payment of the period, without distinguishing capital from revenue or adjusting for timing.

questions.prompt: A life membership fee received by a club should be shown:
options: In the income and expenditure account as income
In the receipts and payments account and then in the capital fund
As a charge against the surplus
questions.answer: In the receipts and payments account and then in the capital fund
questions.explanation: It appears as a receipt in the cash summary and, being capital in nature, is transferred to the capital fund in the balance sheet.

questions.prompt: Subscriptions received ₹2,00,000 including ₹7,000 for next year and ₹4,000 for last year. Income for this year is:
questions.explanation: Deduct the advance of ₹7,000 and the prior-year amount of ₹4,000 from the receipts: 2,00,000 − 7,000 − 4,000 = ₹1,89,000.

questions.prompt: The balance of the income and expenditure account is transferred to:
options: The capital fund in the balance sheet
questions.answer: The capital fund in the balance sheet
questions.explanation: A surplus increases the capital fund and a deficit reduces it, just as net profit adjusts the proprietor’s capital.

questions.prompt: The recurring payment made by a member to retain membership, and the main revenue of such an organisation, is the __________ .
questions.explanation: Subscriptions are the principal recurring income of clubs, societies and institutions and are adjusted for timing each year.

questions.prompt: The excess of expenditure over income for the period in an income and expenditure account is called a __________ .
questions.explanation: A deficit is deducted from the capital fund in the closing balance sheet, whereas a surplus is added to it.

questions.prompt: State four differences between the receipts and payments account and the income and expenditure account.
questions.answer: The receipts and payments account is a cash summary covering both capital and revenue items, with no timing adjustment, while the income and expenditure account is an accrual statement covering revenue items only for the current period. The former shows gross cash inflows and outflows and ends with a cash balance; the latter shows only income earned and expenditure incurred and ends with a surplus or a deficit. The former includes amounts belonging to earlier and later years; the latter excludes them.
questions.explanation: Four differences are required for full marks; describing only the cash versus accrual distinction earns partial credit.

questions.prompt: Give four capital receipts commonly received by a non-trading organisation.
questions.answer: Four capital receipts are life membership fees paid once for permanent membership, legacies received under a will, donations given for a specific durable purpose such as a building or equipment, and proceeds from the sale of an old asset. None of these represents earnings of the period, so each is taken directly to the capital fund in the balance sheet.
questions.explanation: Each item must be identified as capital in nature and excluded from the income and expenditure account.

questions.prompt: Explain how an income and expenditure account is prepared from a receipts and payments account.
questions.answer: Start with the receipts and payments account, which is a cash summary. Take each receipt and decide whether it is capital, which goes to the balance sheet, or revenue, which may belong to this period; deduct receipts relating to earlier years and receipts received in advance for later years, and add amounts earned in this period but not yet received. Take each payment similarly: deduct prepayments relating to a later period, add expenses incurred but unpaid at the year end, and exclude payments for durable assets, which are shown as assets instead. Charge depreciation on assets held. The residue is the surplus or deficit of the period, which is transferred to the capital fund, and every figure removed in this conversion appears in the closing balance sheet.
questions.explanation: The answer must show the direction of each adjustment and end with the link to the capital fund, because the conversion and not the cash summary is what earns marks.

questions.prompt: A club’s receipts show subscriptions of ₹3,60,000; at the year end ₹9,000 is due and ₹6,000 was received in advance. Salaries paid were ₹1,20,000 with ₹5,000 outstanding. Equipment of ₹80,000 was purchased. Calculate the subscription and salary figures in the income and expenditure account and state where the equipment appears.
questions.answer: Subscription income for the year is 3,60,000 + 9,000 − 6,000 = ₹3,63,000: the amount still due has been earned and is added as an asset, while the advance was not earned this year and is shown as a liability. Salary expenditure is 1,20,000 + 5,000 = ₹1,25,000, with ₹5,000 shown as an outstanding liability. The equipment of ₹80,000 is a capital payment: it appears as an asset in the closing balance sheet and only its yearly depreciation would be charged to the income and expenditure account.
questions.explanation: Three separate judgements are tested: adding accrued subscription income, adding the outstanding salary, and keeping the asset purchase entirely out of the accrual statement.
